newsitem.title: USA: Verbal assaults escalate on budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Verbal assaults escalate on budget deal.

text.p: The war of words escalated Thursday over the outlook for a budget deal as the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee said he felt chances of negotiating an agreement with the White House were finished.
"I believe a chance of getting a negotiated budget between the Republicans and the president are finished," Sen. Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said.
Domenici, at an Appropriations panel hearing, complained that the White House talked more about plans to increase spending than about cuts.

Public statements of bipartisan goodwill that started the year have eroded recently, with each party taking shots at the other over lack of visible progress on the budget. Contentious budget negotiations in the last Congress forced two government shutdowns.
Senate Democratic leaders accused Republicans of stalling on budget talks and failing to formulate their own version.
"The Republicans don't have a plan, they only appear to want to criticise the Democrats' plan," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said.
Congressional leaders have been talking privately with administration officials about budget issues, but full-fledged budget negotiations have yet to start.
The White House said it was ready for negotiations to begin. "We're ready to talk now," Lawrence Haas, spokesman for the White House Office of Management and Budget, said.
"We're waiting for the other side to either sit down with us or present an alternative, but the time for carping, it seems to us, is over and the time to work has arrived," he said.

Domenici said Republicans would do a budget: "Just be patient, we'll do one. I'll guarantee that when we're finished it's not going to be a pleasant life for the president, and all these programmes he wants," he said.
He also said there was no alternative to freezing discretionary spending for five years.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott was still aiming to have a budget blueprint crafted by the April 15 deadline, a spokeswoman for the Mississippi Republican said.
On whether Senate Republicans would put together their own budget package, Lott said there were lots of options as to how they would proceed, the spokeswoman said.
House Republican leaders have said the April 15 deadline for a budget resolution would likely be missed and that it would more probably occur in May.

Daschle said Republicans had found a number of excuses for not moving ahead on talks, the latest being discussion on what to do about making the Consumer Price Index more accurate, a move that could potentially cut government outlays.

House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston, a Republican from Louisiana, said he was "disappointed" with a list of 254 programmes that would be terminated under Clinton's budget. "It is not a serious document," he said about the list from the White House budget office.
"What I have been given is a hodgepodge of small programmes, all of which were agreed to by the White House last September as part of our budget agreement," Livingston said.
He called on Clinton to work with Republicans in a "far more constructive, meaningful way to balance the budget. We are off to a poor start."
If Republicans do not like the specifics of Clinton's budget, they should tell the White House what they would change and how they would pay for it, Haas said.

House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich has said all along it would be a difficult process to reach a budget deal, despite a "false sense" among some people that there would be a budget deal by Easter, the Ohio Republican's spokesman said.
"Has anything happened to change his opinion on that? No," the spokesman said.
